rv.q: Vivid, if somewhat unwieldy, British Sign Language version of Mike Bartlett’s disquieting take on workplace dynamics
This version of Bull teaches us that accessibility cannot be an afterthought; it needs to be at the forefront of style and stagecraft.
But the use of sign language brought an extra dimension to proceedings.
I just wish it wasn’t such a grim ordeal to watch.
It may previously have won awards, but in a time of ubiquitous greed and corruption, I struggled to warm to the material.
This production takes us beyond the workplace and challenges us to look further into society – it is confronting, uncomfortable and deeply compelling.
With added artwork projected the means of communication beautifully dovetails with the narrative drive to offer a brutal and unsettling study of how weakness inspires bullying behaviours.
The production loses that hard-earned tension when David Sands’s Carter appears, a character who here becomes too large, losing the tension that sustained anticipation of his arrival has created.

Deafinitely Theatre makes the case for the magic and importance of BSL theatre being for all, and not as an afterthought, introducing me to a new type of theatre that lets language sing through the body.
Once again, Park Theatre has managed to put something genuinely different into its smaller Park90 space.

cn.t: Deafinitely Theatre's BSL adaptation of Bartlett's workplace cruelty drama earns praise for its visceral staging and accessibility innovation, though critics divide on whether the bleak power-play retains its impact over a decade later.
